exercises.prompt: Which social system recognizes individual rights, including property rights, and leaves all property privately owned?

choices.text: Capitalism
A state-run economy that grants favors to selected firms
Anarchy, which rejects every institution that could protect rights
A system in which the public owns each person and his product

feedback.note: Capitalism is the social system based on the recognition of individual rights, including property rights, in which all property is privately owned. Favors and state-run production drop that recognition. Rejecting every protective agency is not the system either, because rights still require a government limited to retaliation. Public ownership of the person is the opposite claim.

exercises.prompt: The clause "all property is privately owned" rules out which arrangement?

choices.text: A person owning what he has produced or earned
Trade between private owners
The state as owner of the means of production
Courts that protect contracts and punish fraud

feedback.note: Private ownership means individuals, not the state, own property, and this matters because trade between owners and courts that protect contracts are part of a system that recognizes property rights. State ownership of the means of production removes "all property is privately owned." Keeping the courts is not state ownership; the courts answer force and fraud rather than taking title.

exercises.prompt: Someone uses the name capitalism for an economy of discretionary licenses and subsidies to favored firms. What is the error?

choices.text: There is no error, because any market word names the system, so favors to firms are capitalism
Subsidies are private property in the state's hands, so a grant to a favored firm is private title
A license is the separation of state and economics, so permission to produce is laissez-faire
Licenses and subsidies are not a system of rights in which all property is privately owned

feedback.note: Discretionary licenses and subsidies replace rights with political favors and give the state a power over production that private ownership does not include. The name capitalism does not stick to that mixture merely because trade still occurs somewhere. A subsidy is not private property, and a license of that kind is the opposite of separating state and economics.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the place it has in the system named here.

pairs.right: Rights recognized, and all property privately owned
Individuals hold title, not the state
Not the system defined by those clauses
The recognition on which the system is based

feedback.note: Capitalism is defined by the recognition of individual rights and by private ownership of all property, and this matters because private ownership means individuals hold title. A controlled economy drops one or both clauses, so it is not the system. Rights are not an optional slogan beside the definition; they are what the system is based on.

feedback.note: Capitalism recognizes rights and private property. State ownership and political favors contradict that recognition: one takes title out of private hands, and the other hands production to pull. Either substitute names a different system. The sentence stays true only while rights and private property remain the defining clauses.

exercises.prompt: A reformer says private ownership of some firms is enough, even if the state owns the rest and directs the whole. What is the error?

choices.text: The system requires that all property be privately owned, not a private corner beside state control
He is right, because rights apply only inside a sector the state chooses to leave alone, not beyond it
State ownership is a form of private property, so a public title to the other firms still counts
Direction by the state is laissez-faire whenever the firms keep their names painted on the door

feedback.note: The definition says all property is privately owned, not that a licensed private corner may sit beside state ownership and state direction. Rights are not a sector the state may shrink. State title is not private title, and a firm's name does not make direction into laissez-faire. The mixture drops the clause that makes the system capitalism.

exercises.prompt: Where does the case for capitalism start?

choices.text: From a taste for busy markets
From individual rights, including property rights
From the goal of making the state wealthy
From an altruist duty to serve a common good

feedback.note: The case for capitalism starts from individual rights, including property rights, because the system is the one that recognizes them. A taste for markets is a brute preference. State wealth treats people as means to the treasury. An altruist common good demands that they live for others. None of those is the moral start; rights are.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the basis of capitalism?
exercises.quote: Capitalism is a social system based on the recognition of individual rights, including property rights, in which all property is privately owned.

choices.text: The system rests on a poll about which policy raises output
The system rests on the state's claim to each person's life
The system rests on the recognition of individual rights, including property rights
Rights are recognized only after officials have finished planning production

feedback.quote: Capitalism is a social system based on the recognition of individual rights, including property rights, in which all property is privately owned.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "What Is Capitalism?," Capitalism: The Unknown Ideal, 19
feedback.note: The passage says capitalism is based on the recognition of individual rights, including property rights. A poll about output is a pragmatist substitute, treating "what works" as the base. The state's claim to the person's life is the opposite of those rights. Planning does not come first: the rights are the basis, and the system is what follows from recognizing them.

exercises.prompt: If individual rights, including property rights, are recognized, which arrangement follows?

choices.text: State ownership, treated as the implementation of those rights
A system of special favors, as the reward of political virtue
No system, because rights are silent about property and production
Capitalism, in which all property is privately owned

feedback.note: Recognizing property rights means people may gain, keep, and use what they produce, so all property is privately owned, and this matters because that is capitalism. State ownership and special favors deny the recognition. Rights are not silent about production: a right is a right to action, and producing is action. The system follows from the rights rather than replacing them.

exercises.prompt: A speaker defends markets only while they raise output, and he will drop them if a controlled economy posts a higher number. What has he left out?

choices.text: The case starts from rights, not from a growth figure
Nothing. Output is the moral base, and rights are a later decoration
He should start from the state's ownership of the person
Rights forbid private property, so the number is all that remains

feedback.note: A growth figure is not the case for capitalism, and this matters because the case starts from rights, so a higher number under compulsion would not justify dropping them. Treating the number as the base is the pragmatist error of asking only what works. State ownership of the person is not the missing premise, and rights do not forbid the property they require.

exercises.prompt: Match each proposed starting point to the standing it has.

pairs.right: The moral start of the case for capitalism
Require private ownership, not a state title

pairs.left: A growth target with no rights
pairs.right: Not the basis of the system
Not the basis; it treats the person as a means

feedback.note: Individual rights are the start, and property rights require that what people produce stay privately owned, and this matters because a growth target without rights can bless any compulsion that posts a number. An altruist common good makes the person a means to others or to the state. Neither rival is the recognition on which capitalism is based.

feedback.note: The case starts from individual rights, because capitalism is the system that recognizes them. Tastes are preferences, quotas are commands, and omens are mystic signs. Any of those substitutes drops the moral principle and treats the system as a liking, a plan, or a revelation rather than as what follows from a person's freedom of action.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle in the order that keeps its meaning.

feedback.note: Capitalism follows from individual rights, and this matters because a growth number is not a moral premise, and state ownership contradicts the property those rights require. Either substitute would give the system a base other than the recognition of rights. The order is rights first, and the private system second.

exercises.prompt: A critic says rights protect speech, but production may be commanded, because action at a workbench is not speech. What is the error?

choices.text: He is right, because only speech is a right and labor is a privilege the state may command at will
Rights are rights to action, including producing and keeping property, not a permit outside them
Commanding production is retaliation against the act of trade, since working was the first force
Property is not among the consequences of the right to life, so earnings fall outside rights

feedback.note: A right sanctions freedom of action, and producing and keeping what one earns are actions. Commanding them initiates force; it is not a zone where rights fall silent, and it is not retaliation, because the producer started none. Speech is not the only right. Property is a consequence of the right to life, so production is inside the case for capitalism, not outside it.

exercises.prompt: What is the moral justification of capitalism?

choices.text: It is a brute preference for faster growth
It serves an altruist common good by using people as means
It is the only system consonant with man's rational nature
It is justified because officials happen to prefer it

feedback.note: Capitalism is justified because it is the only system consonant with man's rational nature: it lets him live by reason, protects his survival as man, and takes justice as its ruling principle. Faster growth, an altruist sacrifice to a common good, and an official's taste are not that justification. They drop the moral fact and leave a preference or a demand that he be used.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about why capitalism is justified?
exercises.quote: The moral justification of capitalism lies in the fact that it is the only system consonant with man's rational nature, that it protects man's survival qua man, and that its ruling principle is: justice.

choices.text: It is justified by sacrificing each man to a collective good, which is what his nature is for
It needs no moral justification, because it is only a preference, and justice does not apply
Its ruling principle is favoritism toward the well connected, so pull replaces what each man earned
It accords with man's rational nature, protects his survival as man, and is ruled by justice

feedback.quote: The moral justification of capitalism lies in the fact that it is the only system consonant with man's rational nature, that it protects man's survival qua man, and that its ruling principle is: justice.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "What Is Capitalism?," Capitalism: The Unknown Ideal, 20
feedback.note: The passage locates the moral justification in three connected facts: capitalism is the only system consonant with man's rational nature, it protects his survival qua man, and its ruling principle is justice, and this matters because survival qua man means life proper to a rational being, not bare subsistence as a means. A collective sacrifice, a mere preference, and favoritism each deny one of those facts.

exercises.prompt: Justice, as the ruling principle of this system, requires which policy?

choices.text: Each person keeps the consequences of his own action, and special favor is ruled out
The state assigns rewards by political pull, and that assignment by connection is justice
The productive are sacrificed to those who produce nothing, as a duty justice imposes
Outcomes are equalized regardless of what anyone did, and that result is justice

feedback.note: Justice gives each person what his own action has earned, so he keeps the consequences and no one receives a special political favor, and this matters because pull, a duty to sacrifice the productive, and equalization apart from action all break that principle. They treat justice as a distribution by need, by power, or by an altruist demand, which is not the ruling principle of capitalism.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase to the role it does or does not play in the justification.

pairs.right: The moral justification of capitalism
Not the justification
Not the justification; it uses the person as a means
The system's ruling principle

feedback.note: The justification is that capitalism accords with man's rational nature. A preference for growth and an altruist common good are the rivals: one has no moral standard, and the other sacrifices the person. Justice is the ruling principle, meaning each person's action carries its consequences. Confusing justice with a collective aim drops the justification.

exercises.prompt: Complete the principle with the term that keeps this claim true.

feedback.note: The ruling principle is justice, because each person must keep the consequences of his own action. Sacrifice hands those consequences away as a duty. Pull hands them to the politically favored. Chance denies that action has consequences that are his. None of those three is the principle that makes the system consonant with a rational life.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle in the order that keeps its meaning.

feedback.note: Capitalism accords with man's rational nature, and this matters because a brute preference drops the moral justification and leaves a taste. An altruist sacrifice makes him a means to others, which contradicts a nature that must live by its own reason. Either substitute would justify him as a tool or as a liker, not as a rational being.

exercises.prompt: A skeptic says capitalism and a controlled economy may be chosen as colors are chosen, since neither is a moral question. What is the error?

choices.text: He is right, because politics stands outside morality, so justice does not apply
The justification is moral: only capitalism accords with man's rational nature
He is right, because both systems equally protect rights, so either choice is just
A preference for control is justice, so production orders are what justice requires

feedback.note: The choice of system is moral because only capitalism is consonant with man's rational nature and with justice. Treating it as a color is the brute-preference error, and skepticism about moral knowledge does not make the systems equal. A controlled economy does not protect rights. A preference for control is not justice; justice is the principle control violates.

exercises.prompt: A defender says capitalism is moral because it makes the group rich and the individual is the means to that group wealth. What is the error?

choices.text: He is right, because justice means group wealth, so using each man as a means to that wealth is the moral justification
Rational nature means the person exists for the nation, so his survival as man consists in service to that collective end
That is an altruist common-good defense; the justification is his nature as a rational being, not his use as a means
A common-good sacrifice is the same claim as the right to one's own life, so giving him up to the group fulfills it

feedback.note: Using the individual as a means to group wealth is an altruist defense, and it is not the moral justification of capitalism, and this matters because the justification is that the system accords with his rational nature and with justice, so he can live for his own sake. The nation is not what his nature exists for. A sacrifice to a common good contradicts the right to his own life rather than restating it.

exercises.prompt: What does laissez-faire mean in this account of capitalism?

choices.text: State direction of economics whenever the cause is called good
Separation of a person from the property he has earned
A license system that hands special favors to selected firms
Separation of state and economics

feedback.note: Laissez-faire means the separation of state and economics, in the same way and for the same reasons as the separation of state and church, and this matters because direction of the economy, taking a person's property, and a system of favors all join the state to production. The separation leaves production and trade to private owners and keeps government at the protection of rights.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the capitalism it names?

A regulated system of favors, with the state directing production and naming it capitalism
The state runs production but is kept out of the churches, and that split is the separation

feedback.quote: When I say "capitalism," I mean a full, pure, uncontrolled, unregulated laissez-faire capitalism—with a separation of state and economics, in the same way and for the same reasons as the separation of state and church.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Objectivist Ethics," The Virtue of Selfishness, 33
feedback.note: The passage means by capitalism a full, pure, uncontrolled, unregulated laissez-faire, with state and economics separated as state and church are separated. That is not regulated favoritism, and it is not "run the economy but spare the churches." Unregulated names the separation from economic control. It does not abolish courts or the protection of contracts, which are not economic direction.

exercises.prompt: Separation of state and economics rules out which pair, and keeps which function?

choices.text: It rules out the police, and it keeps subsidies to favored firms as the function that remains
It rules out economic control and special favors, and it keeps the protection of rights
It rules out private choices of what to produce, and it keeps a planning board in charge
It rules out courts, and it keeps a bureau that sets prices in place of private bargains

feedback.note: Laissez-faire rules out government running of the economy and the granting of special favors. It does not rule out police, courts, or defense, because those protect rights rather than direct production. Private choices of what to produce are what the separation leaves free. A planning board or a price bureau is the control the separation forbids.

exercises.prompt: Match each policy to the side of the separation it falls on.

pairs.left: A subsidy reserved for one favored firm
pairs.right: A special favor, which is ruled out

pairs.left: A law that dictates the production plan
pairs.right: Government running of the economy, which is ruled out
Not ruled out; it is protection of rights

feedback.note: Laissez-faire separates state and economics, and this matters because a subsidy to a favorite and a dictated production plan both put the state into the economy, one by favor and one by running it. Courts that protect contracts from fraud stay on the government's proper side of the line. Calling that protection "economic control" would abolish the protection of rights in the name of laissez-faire.

feedback.note: The separation is between state and economics, because laissez-faire takes the state out of production and trade. Separating the state from property would strip owners of title. Separating it from courts or defense would abolish the protection of rights. Those are not the laissez-faire claim. The state stays, and it stays out of running the economy.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle in the order that keeps its meaning.

feedback.note: Laissez-faire separates state and economics, and this matters because merging them is government running of the economy. Adding favors is the political privilege the separation rules out. Either change would make the phrase mean its opposite. The principle keeps production private and government at the protection of rights.

exercises.prompt: A law bans every competitor of one factory and calls the ban support for capitalism. What is the error?

choices.text: There is no error, because help for a firm is what private property means
Competition is initiated force, so the ban is retaliatory
A ban that protects a favorite is a special favor, which laissez-faire rules out
Separation of state and economics requires bans of this kind

feedback.note: Protecting one factory from competitors is a special favor, and laissez-faire rules favors out along with any government running of the economy. The ban is not private property; it initiates force against other owners. Competition is not force. The separation does not require such bans. It forbids them, for the same reason it forbids a state church: the state does not run that realm.

exercises.prompt: A critic says that keeping the police and the courts already betrays laissez-faire, because a state still exists. What is the error?

choices.text: He is right, because any institution is economic control, so the police already run production
Courts are special favors by definition, so judging a contract is a subsidy to one party
Police work is government running of production, so arresting a thief directs the economy
Laissez-faire separates state and economics; it does not abolish the protection of rights

feedback.note: Laissez-faire is the separation of state and economics, not the abolition of government. Police and courts protect rights by retaliatory force; they do not run production or grant favors. Calling every institution economic control, or calling a court a favor, confuses the proper functions with the controls laissez-faire actually rules out.

exercises.prompt: Which order states the case from its moral start to the social system?

choices.text: Each person is an end in himself; rights follow; laissez-faire capitalism respects those rights
Growth figures come first, rights are optional, and the state may own the person to lift the figures
The state is the end, persons are its means, and favors follow from the state's ownership of them
Capitalism comes first, and rights are whatever surviving firms will allow after they have succeeded

feedback.note: The order is fixed by the moral fact: each person is an end in himself, so he holds rights to his own action, and laissez-faire capitalism is the system that recognizes those rights, including property, and this matters because growth figures, a state that owns him, and firms that invent rights afterward all reverse or drop that order. Rights are not a byproduct of the firms.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish as the moral premise at the start of the political case?
exercises.quote: By the grace of reality and the nature of life, man—every man—is an end in himself, he exists for his own sake, and the achievement of his own happiness is his highest moral purpose.

choices.text: Man exists to be used for the state's ends, and his highest purpose is whatever goal the state assigns to him
Man is an end in himself, exists for his own sake, and his own happiness is his highest moral purpose
Happiness is a whim with no tie to values he has achieved, and the passage treats that whim as the purpose
A person is a means to a common good, and that use is his purpose, so he exists for the group alone

feedback.quote: By the grace of reality and the nature of life, man—every man—is an end in himself, he exists for his own sake, and the achievement of his own happiness is his highest moral purpose.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 123
feedback.note: The passage establishes that every man is an end in himself, exists for his own sake, and that his own happiness is his highest moral purpose. It does not say he exists for the state or as a means to a common good. Happiness here is not a whim; it is the purpose tied to his life. That premise is the start from which rights, and then the system that respects them, follow.

exercises.prompt: If a person is an end in himself and not a means, what does his life require in politics?

choices.text: Ownership of his life by the public, so his action waits on the nation
A duty to be disposed of for a national purpose, with his own ends set by the officials
Rights to action, including property, which laissez-faire capitalism recognizes
Permits that create his freedom only after officials approve the ends he may hold

feedback.note: An end in himself must be free to act for his own life, so he holds rights, including property rights, and the system that respects them is laissez-faire capitalism, and this matters because public ownership, a national claim on him, and permits that create his freedom all treat him as a means whose action waits on someone else. The political requirement follows from the moral premise; it is not a favor added later.

pairs.right: The moral start
The political principle that follows
The system that respects those rights

pairs.left: A state that treats him as a means
pairs.right: The rival that breaks the chain

feedback.note: The chain runs from man as an end, to the rights that sanction his action, to laissez-faire capitalism as the system that recognizes those rights and keeps property private. A state that treats him as a means breaks the chain at the start, because it denies that he exists for his own sake. Later links cannot be saved while that denial stands.

Completing the sentence with any of them would make his life belong to someone else, which is the premise the chain rejects before it ever reaches rights or capitalism.

feedback.note: Because each person is an end, rights follow. If the state is the end, rights do not follow; he becomes a means. If favors follow, the conclusion is political pull rather than a system of rights. The order keeps the person as the end, then the rights, and only then the laissez-faire system that respects them.

exercises.prompt: A planner says, "Adopt capitalism first, and define rights afterward so they fit the firms we like." What is the error?

choices.text: He is right, because firms create rights by being successful, and success is the source
Rights are a brute preference for growth, so the firms the planner likes should write them
Laissez-faire means favors for whichever firms the planner likes, with rights cut to match
The order is reversed: rights come first, and the system is the one that respects them

feedback.note: Rights are not manufactured to fit favored firms. They follow because each person is an end, and capitalism is justified only as the system that recognizes them. Success does not create a right, and growth is not the moral base. Favors for liked firms are what laissez-faire rules out. His order makes the system a primary and the principle a costume.

exercises.prompt: Someone says, "A person is an end, so the government must guarantee him other people's products." What is the error?

choices.text: Being an end sanctions his freedom of action; it is not a claim on other people's products
He is right, because an end must be supplied by other people's effort and by their goods
Other people's products are the fundamental right his standing as an end requires of them
Laissez-faire means the state distributes goods to each person because he is an end

feedback.note: That he is an end sanctions his own freedom of action, from which rights and laissez-faire capitalism follow. It does not entitle him to other people's products, which would make them means to him. Their goods are not the fundamental right, and distribution by the state is not laissez-faire. The chain protects each person's action; it does not issue claims on the others.

exercises.prompt: What counts as physical force in this political sense?

choices.text: A strongly worded argument that the listener finds unpleasant
Compulsion against a person's body or against his property
Any obstacle at all, including a fact of nature
The feeling of pressure that disagreement can produce

feedback.note: Physical force, in politics, is compulsion against a person's body or property, and this matters because a harsh argument and the discomfort of disagreement leave his judgment and his goods intact, so they are not that compulsion. A fact of nature is not a person using force. Treating any of those as force erases the act that actually violates a right.

exercises.prompt: A man locks another man in a room and will not let him leave. What kind of act is that?

choices.text: Only an opinion about where the other man should stay
Economic competition
Physical force against the person
A refusal to deal with him

feedback.note: Locking a man in a room compels his body, so it is physical force against the person. It is not an opinion, because an opinion leaves him free to walk out. It is not competition or a refusal to deal, because those leave his body and his property under his own control. The lock replaces that control.

exercises.prompt: A thief takes a man's earned purse and runs. Which description fits the act?

choices.text: A low offer for the purse
An insult directed at the owner
A metaphysical fact, like a storm damaging a road
Physical force against property

feedback.note: Taking the purse compels the owner's property, so it is physical force even if the thief never strikes him. A low offer and an insult leave the purse in the owner's hands. A storm is not a person initiating force. The theft is a violation because it is compulsion against what the owner holds, not because it is rude.

exercises.prompt: A listener says, "Your argument forced me to change my mind." Has he identified physical force?

choices.text: No, because persuasion leaves the listener's judgment intact
Yes, because any change of mind is compulsion against the body
Yes, because a firm conclusion is the same kind of act as a blow
No, because force names only the acts of a foreign army

feedback.note: Persuasion asks the listener to judge, and he remains free to reject the argument. That is not compulsion against his body or property. Treating a changed mind as a blow confuses evidence with force. Limiting force to foreign armies leaves out the private act, the blow or the seizure, that the principle actually names.

pairs.left: A harsh review of his book

A harsh review does not, because the reader keeps his judgment and his goods. A flood is a fact of nature, not a person initiating force. Calling every loss by one name treats a fact and an insult as if they were compulsion.

feedback.note: Physical force is compulsion against body or property. A strong opinion does not seize either, and a natural fact is not a person's act. Substituting either one would call a right violated where no one has compelled anybody. The principle names compulsion, not offense and not misfortune.

exercises.prompt: A man says a ruined harvest and a robbery are the same kind of force, since both leave him poorer. What is the error?

choices.text: He is right, because every loss is an initiation of force by someone, crop loss included
He treats a fact of nature as if it were compulsion by a person against property

exercises.prompt: Who is it that has no right to use physical force against another person?

Anyone who merely names the starter
The person who starts it
Only a soldier who has crossed a border

Naming the starter is not force at all. Limiting the ban to a foreign soldier would leave domestic initiation out, which the principle does not do.

feedback.note: The passage establishes that no man has the right to initiate the use of physical force against another man. The line is who starts, not who is stronger.

exercises.prompt: A mugger grabs a wallet. The owner pulls it back and holds the mugger for the police. Who initiated force?

Equal touching is a false description, because it drops who began the compulsion. The wallet is property, so the seizure is force against it, not a blank spot in the principle.

exercises.prompt: What is retaliatory force, as against the force that is forbidden?

exercises.prompt: Why is the initiation of physical force the basic political evil?

feedback.note: Starting force is the basic political evil because it replaces the victim's judgment with compulsion, so he cannot act on his own mind. Manners are not that standard. exercises.prompt: What does the initiator take from the victim that a mere disagreement does not take?

choices.text: Control of the victim's own action, by putting compulsion in place of his judgment

feedback.note: Initiated force takes the victim's control of his own action, because compulsion stands where his judgment should stand. A sincere motive does not restore that control. exercises.prompt: A gang says, "Sell to us on our terms or we wreck the shop," and the owner sells. Was that sale an exercise of his judgment?

No, because the threat replaced his judgment with compulsion
Yes, because a sale is voluntary whenever money changes hands

feedback.note: The threat of wrecking the shop replaced the owner's judgment: he did not choose the terms, he submitted to force. A spoken yes under that threat is not an exercise of judgment. Money moving does not make the sale voluntary, and commerce does not sit outside politics when force is what moves it. The evil is the substitution of compulsion for his mind.

exercises.prompt: An official compels a peaceful man "for his own good" and says the motive removes the evil. What is the error?

choices.text: He is right, because a kindly end turns initiation into retaliation against the man he compels

exercises.prompt: How do fraud and a credible threat stand to the initiation of force?

choices.text: They initiate force, because they obtain a value by destroying voluntary consent

feedback.note: Fraud and a credible threat initiate force because each obtains a value by destroying voluntary consent: one by faking the facts, the other by the prospect of physical compulsion. exercises.prompt: A seller hides the fact that the "gold" is painted lead and takes the buyer's money. What has he done?

feedback.note: The seller obtained the money by faking what the buyer relied on, so the buyer's consent was not consent to the actual exchange. That is fraud, and fraud is an initiation of force. It is not a low offer or open competition, because those leave the facts available to the buyer's judgment. It is not a refusal, because the money moved by deceit.

exercises.prompt: An armed man says, "Hand over the money or I will shoot," and he means it. What is that demand?

Words do not make it a joke when the threat is real and is the means of taking the value.

exercises.prompt: The victim of a fraud says he spoke the word yes. A defender answers that the yes was consent, so there was no force. What is the error?

exercises.prompt: What is the right to property, as against a guarantee or a seizure?

It is the right to gain, keep, use, and dispose of what one produces or earns, so a person who owns nothing yet is still free to act and to own the result. Commanding him denies that right. The right does not guarantee that goods are already his; it guarantees that they will be his if he earns them.

exercises.prompt: Which statement is the full claim about property?

choices.text: He may gain, keep, use, and dispose of what he produces or earns, because freedom of action requires that control
A person is guaranteed objects, and he holds a title to what others produce, as freedom's claim on their effort
He may hold goods only as a tenant of the state, because the state owns what he produces and may recall the use
Theft is property whenever the thief needs the goods, because need replaces production and moves the title to him

feedback.note: The full claim joins the right and the reason: a person may gain, keep, use, and dispose of what he produces or earns, because freedom of action requires control of the means and the result. A guarantee of objects, a title to others' products, state tenancy, and need-based theft each drop that claim. They replace his action with a grant, a seizure, or a landlord.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about earning and owning?
exercises.quote: It is not a guarantee that a man will earn any property, but only a guarantee that he will own it if he earns it.

choices.text: He is guaranteed the object whether or not he earns it, success being owed to him
He is not guaranteed to earn property; he is guaranteed to own it if he earns it
Ownership is withdrawn even when he has earned the object, so earning yields no title
Earning creates only a permission, which another person may cancel afterward

feedback.quote: It is not a guarantee that a man will earn any property, but only a guarantee that he will own it if he earns it.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "Man's Rights," The Virtue of Selfishness, 93
feedback.note: The passage draws a precise line: the right is not a guarantee that a man will earn any property, but only a guarantee that he will own it if he earns it. A guaranteed object without earning, a forfeiture after earning, and a cancelable permission all contradict that line. The right protects the consequence of his action. It does not promise the action will succeed, and it does not let others unown what he earned.

exercises.prompt: An artist earns a fee, then is told the fee is society's and he may not spend it. Which part of the right is denied?

choices.text: None. A fee is not a product of effort
Only his dealings with nature, since no person took the fee
Keeping, using, and disposing of what he earned
His duty to seek permission, which is the right working as it should

feedback.note: The fee is the consequence of his work, so it is his property. Forbidding him to spend it denies keeping, use, and disposal together. Calling it society's treats his product as a public title. The taking is a person's or a state's act, not a fact of nature, and a demand for permission replaces the right with a privilege. The whole claim is what the order rejects.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of the right to the act it names.

pairs.right: To produce or earn the value
To own it if he earned it, with no forfeiture
To act on it: consume, sell, or give it
Outside his right

feedback.note: Gaining is producing or earning, and this matters because keeping is owning the result rather than forfeiting it. Use and disposal are the actions on that result. Another person's product stands outside the right, however useful it would be. The four lines together are the claim: control of one's own product, required by freedom of action, and no title beyond it.

feedback.note: If he earns it, he will own it, and this matters because that is the guarantee the right actually gives, and it is not a guarantee that he will earn anything. Forfeit and surrender deny ownership after earning. Borrowing would leave the title with someone else. The principle protects the consequence of his effort and refuses every word that hands that consequence away.

feedback.note: He will own it if he earns it, and this matters because "If he seizes it" would make theft a title. "Whether or not he earns it" would turn the right into a guarantee of an object. Both contradict the principle. Ownership follows earning, and earning is not promised. The sentence keeps that order and no other.

exercises.prompt: A law says you may work, but the product is publicly owned, and you may use a portion only if an office permits. What is this?

choices.text: The implementation of the right to life, because a permit over the product is that control
Laissez-faire, because work is still allowed even though the public owns the product
Retaliation against theft, with the worker cast as the thief for producing
A denial of property and of freedom of action, replacing the right with a permission

feedback.note: If the product is publicly owned and use waits on a permit, the worker cannot keep, use, or dispose of what he earns. That denies property and, with it, the control freedom of action requires. Allowing the motion of work is not laissez-faire and does not implement the right to life. He is not a thief for producing. The law replaces a right with a permission.

exercises.prompt: A man obtained a fee by fraud and says that calling the fee his property respects the right. What is the error?

choices.text: Fraud is not earning; a value taken by destroying consent is not property
He is right, because any possession is the right to property, fraud included
Fraud is a voluntary trade, so the title is ordinary and the fee was earned
The victim's consent is irrelevant to who holds title to the fee that was paid

feedback.note: Property is the right to what one produces or earns, and fraud does not earn. It obtains the fee by destroying the other person's consent, which is an initiation of force. Possession by that means is not a title, and the victim's faked consent does not make a trade. Respecting the right means returning what was taken, not blessing the fraud as ownership.

exercises.prompt: What is statism, as a claim about a person's life?

choices.text: The view that government protects rights and stops there
The view that a person's life belongs to the state
The view that each person owns his own life
Any mention of a police force under objective law

feedback.note: Statism is the political view that a person's life belongs to the state. A government that protects rights and stops there is an agent, not that claim. The right to life says the life is his. A police force under objective law does not, by itself, assert that the state owns him. The name picks out the ownership claim, not the mere existence of government.

exercises.prompt: Statism's distinctive claim is a claim about what?

choices.text: Which retaliatory procedures a court should publish
How a contract between private parties should be worded
Who owns the individual's life
Whether a price is high or low

feedback.note: The distinctive claim is about ownership of the individual's life: statism assigns that life to the state. Court procedure, the wording of a private contract, and the height of a price can all be discussed without that assignment. Treating those topics as the view itself confuses a protective institution, a trade, or a number with the claim that the person belongs to the state.

exercises.prompt: A student says statism is only another name for any government. What is the error?

choices.text: There is no error, because an agent is the same thing as an owner, so government is title to the citizens
There is no error, because the existence of courts is the whole view, so a court is the ownership claim
Protecting rights is ownership of the person, so a government of retaliation still holds title to his life
A government limited to protecting rights is not the claim that the person's life belongs to the state

feedback.note: Statism is not the name of every government. A proper government is an agent whose purpose is to protect rights, and that agency is the opposite of owning the citizens. Courts that answer force do not assert the ownership claim. Calling protection "ownership" erases the line between retaliatory force under law and a state that treats the person as its property.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the political claim it does or does not make.

pairs.right: A person's life belongs to the state
An agent that protects rights and does not own the citizens
The life belongs to the person who has it
Not the same claim as statism

feedback.note: Statism says the life belongs to the state. A proper government does not say that; it is an agent protecting rights. The right to life places the life with the person. Police under objective law can exist inside that protection, so the uniform and the statute are not the ownership claim. The error is to treat every institution as statism.

Completing the sentence with the person states the right to life, which is the claim statism denies. The market does not own him, and a court that protects rights is not an owner. The principle names the state as the claimant, not every institution that exists beside him.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle in the order that keeps its meaning.

feedback.note: Statism says a life belongs to the state. "Belongs to the person" is the right statism rejects. "Is protected and left his" describes a proper government, which does not own him. Either substitute would turn the definition into its opposite. The view's content is the ownership claim, not the mere word government.

exercises.prompt: A speaker says, "I oppose statism, but the nation owns each citizen's life for the public good." What is the error?

choices.text: That ownership claim is statism, whatever name he prefers to avoid
He has described a proper government and nothing more
Public good means consent to protect rights and then to stop
Ownership by the nation is the right to one's own life

feedback.note: If the nation owns the citizen's life, the life belongs to the state, which is statism. Refusing the name does not change the claim, and "public good" does not turn ownership into consent for a limited agent. A proper government does not own him. The right to one's own life is what the sentence denies, not what it restates.

exercises.prompt: A writer defines statism as the wish that people be left free to live their own lives. What is the error?

choices.text: He is right, because the state is only an agent, and the name statism adds no further claim
Statism is the opposite claim: the life belongs to the state, not to the person who lives it
Being left free means the state may dispose of the person, and that disposal is what freedom names
Leaving people free is public ownership of them, so that wish is itself the statist claim

feedback.note: The wish that people be left free is the politics of rights, not statism. Statism holds that the life belongs to the state, so the person is not left to live it as his own. An agent that protects rights does not become statism by being called a state. Freedom is not disposal by the state, and it is not public ownership. The definition has named the rival and called it the view.

exercises.prompt: Under statism, who is the owner of a person's life?

choices.text: The person who lives it
Nobody, because a life cannot be the subject of an ownership claim
The state
Whoever is strongest that day, with no institution required

feedback.note: Statism names the state as the owner of the life, and this matters because the person who lives it is, on this view, not the owner. Saying nobody owns it misses the claim actually being made. Strength without an institution is not the view either: statism assigns the life to the state as an institution, not to a passing bully. The owner in the doctrine is the state.

exercises.prompt: On this view, how does the person stand toward his own life?

choices.text: As an end in himself, free to dispose of it
As a right-holder who needs no one's permission to live
As the owner, with the state only an agent he can dismiss from that role
As someone whose life belongs to the state

feedback.note: Statism does not leave him as an end who disposes of his own life. It says the life belongs to the state, so he holds it for that owner. The right to live without permission is the principle this view rejects. An agent the citizens can limit is a proper government, not the owner statism names. His standing is that of a possession, not of a rights-bearer.

exercises.prompt: A speaker says the individual is only the steward, while the real owner is the state. Is that statism?

choices.text: Yes. It assigns ownership of the life to the state, and the softer word does not change the owner
No. Steward is a gentle word, so the claim cannot be statism, even with the state named as owner
No. A steward is a trader exchanging value for value, so the state's title is only a trade
No. Naming a steward is laissez-faire, since a soft name for state ownership is private title

feedback.note: Calling the person a steward still names the state as the real owner of the life. That is statism. A softer word does not create a different doctrine. A steward is not a trader: he keeps something for someone else rather than owning what he earns. Laissez-faire recognizes his title. This sentence denies it.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase to the owner it names.

pairs.right: The state owns the life

Not an owner; he holds the life for another
Not an owner of the citizens

feedback.note: Statism's owner is the state, and this matters because the right to life names the person. A steward holds the life for the state and therefore is not the owner, whatever courtesy the title suggests. An agent that protects rights is not an owner either, but for the opposite reason: the citizens did not hand their lives over. The question is who holds title, not which word sounds mild.

A trader owns what he earns and exchanges it by right. A sovereign would be the ruler, which is the state's role in this doctrine, not the person's. Steward is the standing left to him.

exercises.prompt: Someone thinks statism is only public ownership of a railroad, while each citizen's life remains his own. What is incomplete?

choices.text: Nothing. The view names railroads and does not speak about lives

A railroad and a person are the same question, so the life was already included

feedback.note: Public ownership of a railroad is not yet the claim that the person's life belongs to the state. Statism's owner-claim is about that life. Owning a road does not settle who owns him, and it does not prove the life remains his. Treating a person and a railroad as the same question skips the doctrine's actual object. The incomplete step is the life.

exercises.prompt: A speaker says that if a person consents to be protected, he has named the state as owner of his life. What is the error?

choices.text: He is right, because agency and ownership are the same relation under two names
Protection is possible only if the life belongs to the protector who is paid to guard it
Consent to an agent that protects rights does not transfer ownership of the life
The owner is whoever is paid to help, so the fee itself is a sale of the person

feedback.note: Consent to protection authorizes an agent for a specific purpose. It does not make the state the owner of the life, and payment for that protection is not a sale of the person. Agency and ownership are different relations: one acts for a right-holder, the other claims the right-holder. Protection does not require the second. The error turns a delegated function into a title.

exercises.prompt: What does the life that statism assigns to the state include?

choices.text: Only his passport, not his labor
Only his speeches, not his hours
A symbol, with work and time left outside the claim
His work, his time, and his choices

feedback.note: The life assigned to the state includes the person's work, time, and choices, because those are how a life is lived. A passport or a symbol is not a substitute for them. Speeches without the hours, or labor with the choices set aside, would be a partial life the doctrine does not leave him. The claim covers the action of living, not a document about it.

exercises.prompt: If the life belongs to the state, the person's work belongs to whom?

choices.text: The state
The worker, as a remainder the ownership claim does not touch
Whoever bids highest, even when the state forbids the sale
No one, because work is not part of a life

feedback.note: Work is part of the life, so if the life belongs to the state, the work belongs to the state. It is not an untouched remainder. A forbidden sale is not a market title hiding underneath. And work is not outside life; it is time and choice spent producing. Leaving work with the worker while "the life" goes to the state is a way of not meaning the claim.

exercises.prompt: A decree says the citizen may think as he likes, but his working hours are the nation's to assign. What does this do?

choices.text: It leaves the life untouched, because his thoughts were declared free of the decree
It claims his work and his time, which are parts of the life assigned to the state
It is only a schedule, and a schedule cannot be a claim on a life or on work
It protects property by assigning him customers the state has picked for him

feedback.note: Assigning his working hours claims his time and his work, which statism includes in the life that belongs to the state. A promise about thoughts does not leave that life untouched, and a schedule of forced hours is not a neutral calendar. Assigning customers is not protection of property. The decree takes the portion of his life in which he acts.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to its place in the life statism assigns to the state.

pairs.right: Included. It is part of the life claimed

feedback.note: Work, time, and choice are included because they are the life a person actually lives. A geological fact is not that life, and claiming it would not be the doctrine. The error to avoid is a narrowed reading on which the state owns a label called "life" while work, hours, and decisions remain the person's. The claim is not that narrow.

The sentence stays true only when all three are included. Dropping choice, or dropping the hours, is a way of softening a claim that is not soft.

exercises.prompt: An official says drafting a man's years is not statism if the decree never uses the word life. What is the error?

choices.text: He is right, because only the word life counts and the years are a separate topic
Time is not part of a person's life, so the draft cannot touch him, however many years it claims
Drafting his years claims his time, which is part of the life the view assigns to the state
A draft is a contract by definition, whatever the man is told, so his years were given by agreement

feedback.note: The years are his time, and time is included in the life statism assigns to the state. Avoiding the word does not avoid the claim. Time is not outside life. A draft he did not agree to is not a contract; a contract is a voluntary exercise of rights, not a seizure of years. The doctrine is identified by what it takes, not by its vocabulary.

exercises.prompt: A planner says the man's choice of work stays his, because the state owns only the product and the hours. What is the error?

choices.text: He is right, because choice floats free of hours and of the product, so owning them spares his choice
A product is not part of work, so owning it leaves the work free, and the hours may be seized as well
Owning the hours protects his freedom to direct his own action, since the schedule is that freedom
Hours and product are the work and the time; taking them takes the choice of what to do with them

feedback.note: If the state owns the hours and the product, the person does not choose how to spend the time or what happens to the result. That is a claim on choice, not a way of sparing it. Choice does not float free of the actions that express it. The product is part of the work. Owning the hours does not protect freedom; it is the denial that the time is his to direct.

exercises.prompt: Why does statism treat the person as a means?

choices.text: Because his life belongs to the state, so he is used for the state's ends
Because it protects him from initiated force and then stops, making him a means
Because he is an end in himself, so the state must spend him to honor that
Because he owns what he earns and may refuse a trade, which makes him the tool

feedback.note: Statism treats him as a means because it holds that his life belongs to the state, and a life that belongs to another is used for that other's ends. Protection that stops at rights does the opposite: it leaves him as an end. Owning what he earns and refusing a trade are exercises of his rights, not the relation of a means. The ownership claim is what makes him a tool.

exercises.prompt: In this claim, what is it to treat a person as a means?

choices.text: To trade with him, value for value, by mutual consent
To use him for ends that are not his own
To act as his agent and only within a delegated purpose
To leave him free to keep the consequences of his own action

feedback.note: A means is someone used for ends that are not his own. Trade, limited agency, and leaving him his product all respect him as an end who acts for himself. Statism's step is the further one: because the life belongs to the state, his work and choices are spent on the state's ends. Calling a trade "use" would smear the distinction the claim actually draws.

exercises.prompt: A speech says, "The citizen exists so that the nation may be great." How does that speech treat him?

choices.text: As an end in himself
As a trader whose own purpose sets the terms
As a means to the nation's ends
As the owner of his life, with the nation as a name for him

feedback.note: If he exists so that the nation may be great, his life is for the nation's ends and he is a means, and this matters because that is what follows when the life belongs to the state. He is not described as an end, as a trader setting his own terms, or as the owner for whom the nation is only a name. Greatness of the nation is the end; he is the material used to reach it.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the place it has in this account.

pairs.left: The life belongs to the state
pairs.right: The reason the person is treated as a means
What the person is used for
The standing statism rejects
Not the relation of a means to an owner

feedback.note: Because the life belongs to the state, the person is a means to the state's ends. An end in himself is the standing this denies. A voluntary trade is not that relation: each party acts for his own sake and neither owns the other. Collapsing trade into "being used" would make every agreement statism, which drops the ownership claim that actually does the work.

feedback.note: The person is treated as a means to the state's ends, because those are the purposes for which an owned life is spent. Rights, contracts, and defense are not "ends" that use him up: rights protect his own action, a contract is his agreement, and defense answers force against him. Substituting those words would describe a proper government, not the use statism makes of him.

The sentence keeps the reason and the result together. Dropping the "because" would make the use of him a brute preference rather than the consequence of who is said to own the life.

exercises.prompt: A theorist says the life can belong to the state while the person remains an end in himself. What is the error?

choices.text: He is right, because ownership and purpose have nothing to do with each other
An end is someone who exists for another's plan, so the state's plan is what makes him an end
Belonging to the state is what makes him an end, because its purpose becomes his sake
If the life belongs to the state, he is used for its ends and is not an end in himself

feedback.note: An end in himself exists for his own sake, and this matters because if the life belongs to the state, he exists for the state's ends, which is the definition of a means. Ownership and purpose are not separable here: the owner's ends are what the life is for. Redefining "end" as someone who exists for another's plan simply renames a means. The two claims cannot be held together.

exercises.prompt: A law commands his career for a public plan. A defender says he is still an end, because no chain is visible. What is the error?

choices.text: The command uses him for the state's ends without a visible chain; the ownership claim is already in the command
He is right, because only iron chains are statism, so a career assigned on paper still leaves him an end
A career is not part of a life, so the command cannot use him, and his working years stay outside that life
A public plan is the right to one's own life under another name, so obedience to the plan is what keeps him an end

feedback.note: A commanded career spends his work, time, and choice on the state's ends. That treats him as a means whether or not a chain is visible. Iron is not the test; the test is who disposes of the life. A career is part of the life. A public plan that seizes it is not the right to his own life. The defender has kept the use and deleted only the hardware.

exercises.prompt: Which wording is the same claim as statism?

choices.text: The government may use force only in retaliation, under objective law
You have a duty to live for the nation
You own your life, and others may not initiate force against you
A contract is an exercise of rights, not a permission that creates them

feedback.note: A duty to live for the nation assigns the life to the nation, which is statism worded as duty rather than as a deed of sale. Retaliatory government, the right to one's own life, and a contract as an exercise of rights are the opposing claims. The duty wording does not become innocent by avoiding the verb "belongs." It still says the life is owed to the state.

exercises.prompt: A charter says, "The public owns the person." What view is that?

choices.text: A statement of the right to one's own life
Laissez-faire capitalism
Statism, worded as public ownership of the person
A rejection of every claim on the person's work, time, and choice

feedback.note: Public ownership of the person is statism in direct language: the life belongs to the public, which means to the state. It is not the right to one's own life, and it is not laissez-faire, which recognizes private rights and does not own the citizen. The sentence is a claim on his work, time, and choice. Calling the owner "the public" rather than "the state" does not change the owner.

exercises.prompt: A program says each citizen's work must serve the national purpose. What does that purpose-language claim?

choices.text: Only a polite slogan, with no claim on action, work, or the time it takes
The duty to respect other people's rights, and nothing that reaches his own work
The duty to keep what one earns, which is all a national purpose can mean
The same surrender of work, time, and choice that ownership by the state names

feedback.note: A national purpose that must be served by his work claims the work, the time it takes, and the choice of what the work is for, and this matters because that is the life assigned to the state, worded as purpose rather than as property. It is not a slogan with no action under it, not the duty to respect others' rights, and not the duty to keep what he earns. Those last two are the politics this wording rejects.

exercises.prompt: Match each wording to the claim it actually makes.

pairs.left: Your life belongs to the state
pairs.right: Statism in direct wording

pairs.left: You owe your life to the nation
pairs.right: The same claim, worded as a duty
The same claim, worded as public ownership of the person

pairs.right: Not statism

"You are an end in yourself" denies that claim. A change of wording, from belongs, to owe, to the public, does not open a new doctrine. The test is whether the life is still assigned away from the person.

"Limits the state to rights" describes a proper government, not a duty to live for the nation. exercises.prompt: A speaker says, "This is not statism; it is patriotism, and it only asks that you spend your career as the nation directs." What is the error?

choices.text: Directing the career for the nation is the ownership claim under another name
He is right, because a new name creates a new doctrine
Patriotism, as he defines it, means the nation is only the individual's agent
A career is neither time nor choice, so the request claims nothing

feedback.note: Spending the career as the nation directs hands over work, time, and choice. That is statism whether it is called patriotism or not. A new name does not create a new doctrine, and his definition is not "the nation is your agent." A career is precisely time and choice at work. The error is to think a favored word can launder the claim that the life belongs to the nation.

exercises.prompt: A program says, "Nobody owns you. You are simply obligated to give your labor, your years, and your decisions to the public whenever it asks." What is the error?

choices.text: There is no error, because avoiding the word ownership avoids the claim on his labor and years
The obligation is public ownership of his work, time, and choice, with the word ownership avoided
The error is that he described a contract the person freely made, rather than an order he never accepted
He has restated the right to one's own life, since labor and years given to the public are that right

feedback.note: An obligation to hand labor, years, and decisions to the public whenever it asks is a claim on work, time, and choice. That is the life belonging to the public, which is statism, and deleting the word ownership does not delete the claim. It is not a contract, because nothing was agreed. It is not the right to one's own life. The wording is the doctrine in a softer voice.
